title: Own-authority truckload freight brokerage for small/mid Midwest shippers (dry van)
product_service: Arranging full-truckload dry-van moves for shippers using vetted third-party carriers; quoting, tendering, tracking, billing, claims handling.
target_customer: Logistics/shipping managers or owners at small-to-mid manufacturers, distributors and CPG/packaging companies ($5M-$300M revenue) without large-broker attention; Midwest origin lanes.
purchase_motivation: Need reliable capacity on short notice, spot coverage when contract carriers reject, price, service responsiveness.
spending_evidence: Very large existing spend: C.H. Robinson NAST alone billed $3.83B in Q3 2026 [A, WS07-S008]; RXO brokerage $1.43B in Q3 2026 [A, WS07-S010]; FMCSA estimate implies ~33,000 registered brokers in 2022 [A-derived, WS07-S001].
representative_operators: C.H. Robinson — NAST revenue $3.83B Q3 2026, AGP ~13.5% of revenue [A, WS07-S008]
RXO — brokerage GM 12.6% Q3 2026; being acquired by CHR ($5.8B) [A, WS07-S010]
Landstar — agent model, purchased transportation 78.2% of revenue [A, WS07-S011]
TQL, Echo, Arrive, Uber Freight — large privately held/private-equity peers (sizes not verified)
revenue_mechanism: Spread between shipper rate and carrier pay per load (gross margin), plus accessorials.
typical_transaction_value: Incumbent truck revenue ~$2,811/load (Landstar Q3 2026) [A, WS07-S011]; incumbent AGP ~13.5% => ~$300-$400 gross per load [A-derived, WS07-S008]; new entrant spot loads 10-20% margin [E].
direct_costs: Carrier linehaul pay (82-90% of revenue), load-board/TMS subscriptions, carrier-vetting tools, factoring/quick-pay cost, cargo-claim deductibles, bad debt.
contribution_profit_note: ~$250-$400 gross per load at 12-15% on ~$2,500 loads [E, anchored on A comps]; after factoring (~2%/30 days of invoice, WS07-S017 D) and tools, ~$180-$330 contribution per load [E].
working_capital_note: Structural negative: incumbent CHR carries ~61 days of receivables vs ~39 days payables [A-derived, WS07-S009]; shippers pay 30-60+ days while small carriers expect quick pay [D, WS07-S017]. At $250k/month revenue a new broker funds roughly $150k-$250k of carrier pay or pays ~1-5%/30 days to a factor [E]. BMC-85 route ties up $75k cash/ILOC [A, WS07-S001]; BMC-84 route depends on personal credit for premium/collateral [E].
sales_cycle: Spot quotes same-day; becoming a routing-guide/backup carrier 1-6 months; primary contract lanes require RFP cycles (annual).
repeat_purchase: recurring — shippers tender weekly/daily once a broker is in the routing guide
customer_accessibility: Shippers are identifiable (manufacturer databases, import records) and reachable by phone; but they are bombarded by broker cold calls and credibility/track record gates primary freight.
supplier_accessibility: Confirmed abundant carrier supply via load boards historically (>70,000 capacity providers at Landstar alone [A, WS07-S012]), but capacity tightened in 2026 as non-domiciled/ELP enforcement removed drivers [C, WS07-S014, WS07-S015].
competitive_intensity: extreme — tens of thousands of brokers, consolidation (CHR acquiring RXO), AI-enabled incumbents cutting headcount (NAST -11.4% YoY) [A, WS07-S008].
entry_strategy: Lane-density focus (e.g., a few Chicago-outbound corridors) and 24/7 responsiveness for shippers too small for large-broker account teams; start as agent (WS07-002) to build book before own authority.
licenses: FMCSA property-broker operating authority via Motus (identity proofing; min. 8 business days review) [A, WS07-S002]; OP-1 filing fee reportedly $300 [D, WS07-S005]; $75,000 financial security on BMC-84 surety bond or BMC-85 trust limited since 2026-01-16 to cash/ILOC/Treasuries [A, WS07-S001]; BOC-3 process agent filing [A, WS07-S002]; UCR $46 (2026) rising to $55 (2027) [A, WS07-S003, WS07-S004]; contingent cargo + general liability insurance not federally mandated but shippers usually require it [E]; no Illinois property-broker license identified [E, not verified].
regulatory_barriers: Immediate-suspension rule: if bond/trust drawn below $75k and not replenished within 7 calendar days of FMCSA notice, authority is suspended [A, WS07-S001]; broker-transparency (371.3) supplemental proposal pending at OIRA [C, WS07-S007]; negligent-selection liability exposure (case law, not reviewed) [E].
operational_risks: Double-brokering, fictitious pickups and identity-theft carriers; cargo-theft losses ~$725M in 2025 (+60%) with schemes using acquired carriers [C, WS07-S016]; service failures on tight-capacity days.
financial_risks: Shipper insolvency/bad debt; margin squeeze when contracted sell rates lag carrier cost (CHR cost/mile +33.5% vs rate +31.5%) [A, WS07-S008]; bond drawdown from unpaid carrier claims; factoring recourse.
geographic_constraints: None legally; Chicago lanes give density; can serve nationally by phone.
founder_expertise: Freight pricing, lane knowledge, carrier vetting/fraud screening, credit control, TMS use; selling to shipping managers.
staffing: Founder sells and books initially; first hire carrier sales/ops rep at ~$40-60k + commission once ~5-10 loads/day [E].
automation_potential: Rate quoting from benchmarks, carrier outreach/email parsing, track-and-trace updates, document/invoice matching, carrier identity screening — real but incumbents (CHR AI agents) already deploy it.
delegation_potential: Moderate-high: broker reps are a standard labor market; book-of-business key-person risk remains.
scalability: Add reps and lanes; mature small brokerages run many desks; ceiling large but returns decline as competition grows.
expansion: LTL, reefer, flatbed, drayage, managed transportation, warehousing partners, freight audit.
roic_note: Asset-light but working-capital-heavy; if $50-100k is at risk (bond collateral + WC) and op profit ~$100k, ROIC ~100-200% [E]; factoring lowers capital but takes ~10-15% of gross margin [E].
critical_assumptions: New entrant can achieve 12-18% margins on mostly spot/transactional freight
Founder can win 3-10 shipper accounts in year 1 by cold outreach
Founder personal credit qualifies for affordable BMC-84 bond (else $75k BMC-85)
Fraud losses can be kept below ~1% of revenue with vetting tools
unanswered_questions: Primary-source confirmation of the $300 OP-1 fee (FMCSA site blocked)
Census SUSB firm-size distribution for NAICS 488510 (not retrieved)
Current BMC-84 premium ranges by credit tier
Survival rate of new broker authorities after 2-3 years
failure_modes: Never gets past spot quoting into routing guides
One shipper default wipes out a year of margin
Double-brokered/stolen load leads to claim and bond drawdown
Rate spikes squeeze committed sell rates
Founder cannot hire reps who retain books

title: Recurring residential cleaning company (W-2 team model, biweekly plans)
product_service: Scheduled weekly/biweekly/monthly whole-home cleaning by 2-person W-2 teams, plus deep cleans and move-in/out cleans.
target_customer: Dual-income and affluent households (often $100k+ income) in Chicago suburbs and dense city neighborhoods.
purchase_motivation: Time savings, consistency, trust (bonded/insured vetted staff vs. independent cleaners).
spending_evidence: MaidPro 245 franchises averaged $430,998 gross consumer sales in 2025 (median $380,083; ~2,423 jobs/unit) [B, WS18-S004]; Molly Maid average $173.43 per cleaning and 91% of cleanings for recurring customers in 2024 [B, WS18-S002]; 432 Molly Maid US franchises open end-2025 [B, WS18-S003].
representative_operators: Molly Maid (Neighborly) — 432 US franchises, ~$173/clean average [B, WS18-S002/S003]
MaidPro — 245 reporting franchises, avg $431k sales [B, WS18-S004]
The Maids — large franchise system (Item 19 not retrieved)
Thousands of independent owner-operators and solo cleaners (not quantified)
revenue_mechanism: Price per visit (flat or hourly) × visits; recurring plans billed per visit to card on file.
typical_transaction_value: ~$150-$230 per recurring clean (Molly Maid avg $173.43, MaidPro ≈$178/job) [B]; recurring client ≈ $3,500-$5,000/yr at biweekly frequency [E].
direct_costs: Cleaner wages + payroll taxes + workers' comp (largest cost), drive time/mileage, supplies, damage claims.
contribution_profit_note: Assumed labor 45-55% of revenue for W-2 team model; contribution ≈$60-90 per $175 clean before marketing and office [E]. No franchisor cost data captured.
working_capital_note: Card charged at/after each visit; payroll biweekly — minimal receivables. Main cash need is payroll during ramp and marketing.
sales_cycle: Days: online quote → first clean within 1-2 weeks.
repeat_purchase: recurring — 91% of Molly Maid cleanings are for recurring customers [B, WS18-S002]
acquisition_channels: Direct mail to high-income zip codes
customer_accessibility: High — households search actively and switch easily; affluent zip codes identifiable from Census data.
supplier_accessibility: Confirmed — supplies are commodity retail/wholesale; binding constraint is labor supply, not goods.
competitive_intensity: high — national franchises plus very large informal/independent cleaner supply undercutting on price.
entry_strategy: Reliability and vetted W-2 staff at mid-premium price; instant online quoting/booking; same team every visit; target suburbs where franchise territories are thin.
licenses: No Illinois state licence for house cleaning; house cleaning is not 'home repair and remodeling' [A, WS18-S010]. Needs entity registration, possibly municipal business licence (Chicago/suburb specifics MISSING), workers' comp (mandatory for employees in IL), general liability and janitorial bond.
regulatory_barriers: Low. Employment-law exposure (worker classification, Illinois paid leave, Chicago minimum wage) is the main regulatory risk.
operational_risks: Cleaner turnover and no-shows, theft/damage allegations, quality consistency, scheduling churn.
financial_risks: Payroll grows ahead of revenue; customer churn requires constant marketing; wage inflation.
geographic_constraints: Route density matters; serve a 15-20 mile radius per office.
founder_expertise: Hiring/training hourly workers, quality-control systems, local digital marketing.
staffing: Hire 2-4 cleaners in month 1-3; office/scheduling manager at ~$300-400k revenue; team leads per 3-4 teams.
automation_potential: Online instant quoting, routing/scheduling optimization, AI call/text intake, review management, applicant screening. Cleaning itself stays manual.
delegation_potential: Good — franchise systems run with owner-managers and office managers; standard hourly roles.
scalability: Moderate: multi-territory metro operator to ~$1-3M revenue (top MaidPro quartile averaged $925k [B, WS18-S004]); labor-limited.
expansion: Move-out/realtor cleans, Airbnb turnovers, post-construction cleaning, window cleaning add-on, adjacent suburbs.
roic_note: Capital at risk ~$20-50k including ramp losses; yr3 profit $40-140k → roughly 150-400% annual return on capital [E].
critical_assumptions: Labor cost ≤55% of revenue in Chicago market at ~$18-22/hr wages
Can recruit and retain reliable cleaners faster than demand grows
Customer acquisition cost recoverable within ~3 months of recurring service
unanswered_questions: Operating margin data for franchise or independent maid services (no Item 19 cost data captured)
Municipal business licence requirements in target suburbs and Chicago
failure_modes: Owner becomes the backup cleaner and scheduler; burnout
Underpricing to compete with informal cleaners leaves no margin

revenue_mechanism: Tuition per course/package; CE packages; brokerage group contracts.

licenses: IDFPR Education Provider license ($1,050) + $150 per course; licensed instructors; registered entity [A, WS09-S006].
regulatory_barriers: Course approvals, proctoring rules, instructor licensing; single published fee schedule for all students [A, WS09-S006].

expansion: Appraiser/leasing agent/managing broker courses; mortgage and insurance prelicense cross-sell.

Brokerages will private-label CE

Whether national online schools already partner for in-person hours

Commercial real-estate brokers for new openings

geographic_constraints: Chicago metro density helpful; Illinois-specific law.
founder_expertise: Hospitality coverage forms, dram shop law, E&S placement.
automation_potential: Renewal remarketing, COI/event certificates; moderate.
scalability: Regional; capped by restaurant churn and E&S capacity.
expansion: Special-event liability online, venue programs, payments cross-sell.

critical_assumptions: Liquor liability markets available to start-up via wholesaler
Average commission >= $1,200/account

title: CDL driver staffing / driver leasing to private fleets and shippers

spending_evidence: MISSING for driver-staffing spend specifically; general industrial staffing growth +7% 2026 [C, WS12-S014].
representative_operators: National driver-staffing operators exist (e.g., divisions of large staffing groups) — not verified this session [E]

IL WC rates for driver classes (7228/7229/7219)

title: Sales/use tax reverse audit (overpayment recovery) for manufacturers and other heavy purchasers
product_service: Review purchase invoices, fixed-asset ledgers, utility bills and use-tax accruals to find tax paid on exempt items (e.g., manufacturing machinery & equipment, production inputs, resale, out-of-state deliveries), then prepare refund/credit claims (or vendor refund requests) with documentation; fee from recovered tax.
target_customer: CFO/controller at manufacturers, printers, distributors and other companies with >$10M/yr taxable purchases, starting in Illinois and neighboring states.
purchase_motivation: Cash refunds with no upfront cost; vendors routinely over-collect on exempt purchases.
spending_evidence: CPA firms market reverse audits to manufacturers and claim manufacturers average $75k+/yr in overpaid sales/use tax [D, WS14-S009]; contingent fees on net tax recovered are common [C, WS14-S010]; findings-based fees restricted in some jurisdictions and for public companies [D, WS14-S029].
representative_operators: Cherry Bekaert - CPA firm reverse-audit practice [D, WS14-S009]
CliftonLarsonAllen - reverse audits/utility refund studies [D, WS14-S029]
Big-4 and regional CPA SALT practices (KPMG, Andersen) - incumbents, fees unknown [D]
revenue_mechanism: Contingency % of net tax refunded/credited (market % MISSING; analyst expectation 20-40%) [E]; some hourly/flat hybrids [C, WS14-S010].
typical_transaction_value: Illustrative: $75k/yr overpaid [D] x ~3-yr lookback = ~$225k refund x 25% = ~$56k one-time fee per client [E].
direct_costs: Analyst/reviewer time, document retrieval, occasional tax-attorney review for contested claims.
working_capital_note: Long cash lag: fee earned only when IDOR/vendor pays or credits (often 6-18 months) [E]; requires funding 6-12 months of operations.
sales_cycle: 2-6 months; requires NDA and access to AP/ERP data.
repeat_purchase: occasional: lookback once, then periodic re-reviews every 2-3 yrs; can convert to ongoing exemption-certificate/accrual monitoring retainer.
acquisition_channels: Outbound to manufacturer CFOs (Illinois Manufacturers' Association directories)
Partnerships with small CPA firms lacking SALT depth
customer_accessibility: Buyers identifiable; credibility wall vs. CPA firms; data access is the hurdle.
supplier_accessibility: N/A.
competitive_intensity: moderate - CPA SALT practices and specialist recovery firms, but mid-market manufacturers are under-served [E].
entry_strategy: Specialize in one exemption cluster (e.g., Illinois manufacturing M&E and production-related purchases) and offer no-cost assessment; partner with small CPA firms that refer and review.
licenses: No license needed to prepare claims: Illinois IL-2848 accepts a non-attorney/non-CPA 'other' POA (with witness/notary step), but an attorney must represent in IDOR administrative hearings or the Independent Tax Tribunal [A, WS14-S008]. Other states' rules vary.
regulatory_barriers: Contingent-fee restrictions in some jurisdictions/for public companies [D, WS14-S029]; claim statutes of limitation (Illinois lookback length to verify) [E]; vendor-refund route needed where tax was paid to vendors [E].
operational_risks: Technical errors in exemption interpretation lead to denied claims or audit exposure for client; contested claims need attorneys.
financial_risks: Long payout lag; claims denied after work done; concentration in few large wins.
geographic_constraints: Start Illinois/Midwest; multi-state possible with state-specific knowledge.
founder_expertise: Illinois ROT/use tax exemptions, claim procedures, audit evidence standards - 3-6 months of study plus mentorship.
staffing: Reviewer analysts (ex-AP/tax staff) after first wins; contract tax attorney for disputes.
automation_potential: High: AI extraction/classification of invoice line items against exemption rules; humans validate and argue claims.
delegation_potential: Analyst-delegable with SOPs; tax judgment stays with senior reviewer.
scalability: Regional to national with state modules; reinvestment in analysts.
expansion: Use-tax compliance monitoring retainer, utility-tax refund studies, other states, property-tax (where non-attorney allowed).
roic_note: Capital is working capital for a 6-12 month cash lag (~$20-60k incl. founder runway); payoffs large per engagement.
critical_assumptions: Mid-market Illinois manufacturers have material overpayments not already recovered
Illinois lookback and claim procedures allow recovery of 2-3+ years
Clients accept ~25% contingency from a non-CPA firm
unanswered_questions: Illinois claim-for-credit limitation period and purchaser vs. vendor refund mechanics
Whether non-CPA firms face reputational barriers with CFOs
failure_modes: Long payout lag starves the firm
Technical mistakes cause denials or client audits
CPA firms bundle reverse audits into existing relationships
